note: Second-pass CRE Set 3 items. Not copied from Set 2. Each display equation is on its own line.

questions.stem:
Life is Weibull. The hazard function is
\[
h(t)=(\beta/\eta)(t/\eta)^{\beta-1}
\]
What is the hazard rate at 500 hours?
questions.why: Use the shape minus one, not the shape, as the time exponent. \[ t/\eta=500/1000=0.5 \] \[ h(500)=(2/1000)(0.5)=0.0010 \] 0.0005 multiplies by \((t/\eta)^{\beta}\). 0.0020 stops at \(\beta/\eta\). 0.5000 is the time ratio. B. 0.0010 per hour

traps.A: Raises the time ratio to beta instead of beta minus one.

chart.title: Weibull hazard inputs
chart.altText: Shape beta is 2. Characteristic life eta is 1,000 hours. The hazard is asked at 500 hours.

questions.stem:
Strength is normal with the parameters below. A unit fails if strength is below the lower specification. The standard-normal tail probabilities are given.
\[
z=(L-\mu)/\sigma
\]
What fraction of units fall below the specification?
questions.why: The standardized distance is \(-2.00\), so the fraction failed is the lower-tail probability at that value. \[ z=(180-200)/10=-2.00 \] The table gives that tail as 0.0228. 0.0505 is the tail at \(-1.64\). 0.9772 is the fraction above the specification. 2.00 is the standardized distance, not a proportion. A. 0.0228

traps.B: Reads the tail for a different standard-normal value.
traps.C: Reports the fraction that meets the specification.

chart.title: Strength and normal tails
chart.altText: Mean strength is 200, standard deviation is 10, and the lower specification is 180. The lower-tail probability at z = -2.00 is 0.0228. The lower-tail probability at z = -1.64 is 0.0505.

questions.stem:
A repairable unit has the mean lives below. Inherent availability excludes logistics delay.
\[
A_i=\frac{MTBF}{MTBF+MTTR}
\]
What is the inherent availability?
questions.why: Add the mean repair time to the mean time between failures, then divide. \[ A_i=\frac{480}{480+20}=0.9600 \] 0.0417 divides repair time by the mean time between failures. 0.9583 subtracts that ratio from 1. 24 divides the two means in the other order. C. 0.9600

chart.title: Inherent availability inputs
chart.altText: Mean time between failures is 480 hours. Mean time to repair is 20 hours. Logistics delay is excluded.

questions.bok: Sources and uses of reliability data
questions.stem:
Field records give a total unit time \(T\) and a failure count \(r\). The times are complete. The point estimate of MTBF is
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{T}{r}
\]
What is that estimate?
questions.why: Divide the total unit time by the number of failures. \[ \hat\theta=\frac{2500}{5}=500 \] 0.002 hours is the failure rate, \(r/T\). 250 hours divides by twice the failure count. 2,500 hours is the total time. C. 500 hours

traps.A: Inverts the ratio and reports the failure rate.
traps.B: Divides by twice the number of failures.

chart.title: Field exposure
chart.altText: Total unit time is 2,500 hours. Five failures were observed. There is no censoring in this total.

questions.stem:
Path A is two independent units in series. Path B is a third independent unit. The function works if either path works.
\[
R_A=R_1 R_2
\]
\[
R=1-(1-R_A)(1-R_B)
\]
What is the mission reliability?
questions.why: Reduce the series path first, then combine the two paths in parallel. \[ R_A=(0.90)(0.90)=0.81 \] \[ R=1-(1-0.81)(1-0.80)=0.962 \] 0.648 multiplies all three reliabilities. 0.810 stops at Path A. 0.998 treats all three units as one parallel group. C. 0.962

traps.D: Ignores the series connection inside Path A.

chart.title: Two-path block diagram
chart.altText: Path A has unit 1 and unit 2 in series, each with mission reliability 0.90. Path B is unit 3 with mission reliability 0.80. Either path can carry the function.

questions.stem:
One unit operates and an identical unit is in cold standby. The switch works with probability \(p\) when it is needed. Use \(e^{-1}=0.3679\). At the mission age, \(\lambda t=1\).
\[
R(t)=e^{-\lambda t}(1+p\lambda t)
\]
What is the mission reliability?
questions.why: The switch probability multiplies only the standby term. \[ R(t)=0.3679(1+0.9)=0.6990 \] 0.3679 ignores the standby. 0.6004 is an active parallel pair. 0.7358 treats the switch as perfect. C. 0.6990

chart.title: Cold standby with an imperfect switch
chart.altText: Lambda t is 1. The switch succeeds with probability 0.90. The spare does not fail while waiting.

questions.stem:
High-cycle fatigue follows the stated S-N relation. \(N\) is cycles to the failure criterion, \(S\) is stress amplitude, and \(b\) is the given exponent.
\[
N_2=N_1\left(\frac{S_1}{S_2}\right)^{b}
\]
How many cycles are expected at the higher stress?
questions.why: The stress doubled, and the life uses the cube of that ratio. \[ N_2=5000\left(\frac{80}{160}\right)^{3} \] \[ N_2=5000(0.125)=625 \] 1,250 squares the ratio. 2,500 uses the ratio once. 40,000 inverts the ratio and cubes it. A. 625

traps.C: Uses the stress ratio without the exponent.

chart.title: S-N fatigue model
chart.altText: At a stress amplitude of 80 MPa the life is 5,000 cycles. The new amplitude is 160 MPa. The exponent b is 3.

questions.stem:
Two redundant channels use the beta-factor model. \(q\) is the failure probability of one channel and \(\beta\) is the common-cause fraction.
\[
Q=(1-\beta)q^{2}+\beta q
\]
What is the probability that both channels are lost?
questions.why: Add the independent double failure to the common-cause term. \[ (1-\beta)q^{2}=0.9(0.05)^{2}=0.00225 \] \[ \beta q=0.1(0.05)=0.00500 \] \[ Q=0.00225+0.00500=0.00725 \] 0.00250 is \(q^{2}\) with no beta split. 0.00500 is only the common-cause term. D. 0.00725

traps.A: Keeps only the independent double-failure term.
traps.B: Squares the channel probability and ignores beta.

chart.title: Beta-factor inputs
chart.altText: Each channel has failure probability 0.05. The common-cause fraction beta is 0.10. The model is for loss of both channels.

questions.stem:
A Crow-AMSAA model gives the cumulative failure count, not the instantaneous intensity.
\[
N(T)=\lambda T^{\beta}
\]
How many failures are expected by 100 hours?
questions.why: Raise the total time to beta, then multiply by the scale. Do not use the instantaneous formula. \[ 100^{0.5}=10 \] \[ N(100)=0.8(10)=8 \] 0.04 is \(\lambda\beta T^{\beta-1}\). 0.80 is the scale. 80 multiplies the scale by the total time. C. 8

traps.D: Multiplies the scale by the total time.

chart.title: Crow-AMSAA cumulative model
chart.altText: Lambda is 0.8, beta is 0.5, and the total time is 100 hours. The question asks for the cumulative failure count.

questions.stem:
A series system has unreliability budget \(Q_s\). Element unreliability is apportioned in proportion to the weights \(w_i\). \(W\) is the sum of the weights.
\[
Q_i=Q_s\frac{w_i}{W}
\]
What reliability is required for the element of weight 3?
questions.why: Give that element three fifths of the unreliability budget, then convert to reliability. \[ Q_3=0.10(3/5)=0.06 \] \[ R_3=1-0.06=0.94 \] 0.9000 copies the system reliability onto the element. 0.9667 splits the budget into three equal parts and ignores the weights. 0.9800 is the reliability of a weight-1 element. B. 0.9400

traps.A: Assigns the system reliability to the element.
traps.D: Uses the allocation for a weight of 1.

chart.title: Weighted unreliability budget
chart.altText: The system unreliability budget is 0.10. Three series elements have weights 1, 1, and 3.
